To develop and validate a questionnaire-free model for severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) using objective parameters from routine checkups, facilitating screening in primary care settings. This retrospective study analyzed 271 snoring participants who underwent polysomnography at a Chinese tertiary hospital (June 2018-June 2024). Participants were categorized into mild-to-moderate (n = 128) and severe (n = 143, apnea-hypopnea index ≥ 30 events/h) OSA groups. The candidate predictors were sex, waist circumference, and the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index. A logistic regression model was developed, internally validated via 1,000 bootstrap resamples, and temporally validated in a 2025 cohort (n = 82). Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Male sex (odds ratio (OR) = 3.69, 95% CI: 1.421-9.583), waist circumference (OR = 1.039, 95% CI: 0.995-1.085; P = 0.081, 95% CI crossing 1), and TyG index (OR = 1.421, 95% CI: 1.028-1.965) were retained in the model. Male sex and the TyG index were independent predictors of severe OSA, whereas waist circumference showed a borderline, non-significant association and should not be interpreted as a statistically significant independent predictor. In the training set, the model yielded an AUC of 0.751 (95% CI: 0.675-0.827), with an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.739 after bootstrap internal validation. In the temporal validation cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.648 (95% CI: 0.525-0.770). At a cutoff of 0.238, sensitivity was 87.2% and negative predictive value was 68.4%. Decision curve analysis demonstrated that the model provided higher net benefit than either the "treat all" or "treat none" strategies across most threshold probabilities (0.07-0.93). This simple, questionnaire-free model offers a favorable net clinical benefit and remains highly sensitive at a low cutoff. It may serve as an adjunctive screening aid to help prioritize patients for PSG, particularly in resource-limited primary care and health examination settings. However, given its modest temporal validation AUC (0.648) and low specificity (38.2%), it should not be used alone to rule out severe OSA.

papers.title: Lavender aromatherapy for rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder: a retrospective case series.
papers.abstract: Some patients with rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) remain refractory to pharmacological treatment. Lavender aromatherapy has been reported to improve sleep quality, but its effects on RBD remain unclear. In this study, we investigated the potential role of lavender aromatherapy as an adjunctive treatment for RBD. We retrospectively reviewed nine patients with difficult-to-manage RBD who had been informed about lavender aromatherapy as a complementary option. All patients underwent polysomnography (PSG) before the initiation of pharmacological treatment to confirm the diagnosis of RBD. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Patient Global Impression of Change (PGI-C) scale and follow-up clinical interviews. Improvement (i.e., PGI-C score of 1-3) was observed in seven of nine patients (78%). Reported benefits included reduced dream-enactment behaviors and improved sleep quality. Olfactory dysfunction was common, although some patients with impaired olfaction also showed clinical improvement. Lavender aromatherapy may serve as a simple adjunctive treatment option for RBD. Further studies are warranted to determine its potential therapeutic role.

papers.title: Sleep Health: The Neglected Third Pillar of Global Health.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental biological requirement and a modifiable determinant of health, yet it remains largely neglected in global public health policy. Despite strong evidence linking insufficient sleep and sleep disorders to adverse cardiometabolic, mental health, developmental, safety, and productivity outcomes, sleep continues to be excluded from most major global non-communicable disease frameworks and from broader Sustainable Development Goal 3 implementation strategies. In this commentary, we argue that sleep should be recognized as a core pillar of health alongside nutrition and physical activity. We synthesize evidence demonstrating that sleep deficiency contributes to a wide range of chronic diseases, road traffic injuries, reduced quality of life, lost productivity, and increased health-care expenditures. We further highlight how sleep disturbances follow marked social, environmental, and political gradients, disproportionately affecting populations exposed to poverty, overcrowding, conflict, displacement, shift work, and climate-related nighttime heat. These inequities are especially relevant in low- and middle-income countries and in heat-vulnerable regions such as the Middle East and North Africa. We also discuss how emerging evidence links climate change to worsening sleep duration, sleep quality, and obstructive sleep apnoea burden, thereby expanding the significance of sleep within climate-health discourse. Beyond describing the problem, we propose practical strategies for implementation, including integrating sleep education into public health campaigns, expanding screening and first-line treatment pathways in primary care, promoting institutional interventions such as delayed school start times, and leveraging digital tools while addressing equity concerns. Finally, we call for the 2026 United Nations High-Level Meeting and related World Health Organization mechanisms to adopt a Sleep Health Equity and Resilience agenda focused on surveillance, workforce development, and context-specific, low-cost interventions. Elevating sleep within global health policy may yield broad co-benefits across multiple priority domains and reduce avoidable health inequities worldwide.

papers.title: Strategies to establish a biologically defined Parkinson's disease cohort prior to the onset of clinically significant motor symptoms.
papers.abstract: Identifying individuals at risk for neurodegeneration is a priority for clinical trials. Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) deploys strategies to enroll individuals before typical clinical Parkinson's disease symptoms: recruiting polysomnogram-confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and central identification of hyposmia via smell testing. Groups were divided into RBD with and without hyposmia (RBD+Hyposmia, RBD-Hyposmia) and hyposmia with and without self-reported dream enactment behavior (Hyposmia + DEB, Hyposmia-DEB). Participants underwent clinical and biomarker testing including CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (CSFaSynSAA) and dopamine transporter imaging. While all enrollment strategies showed robust enrichment for CSFaSynSAA positivity, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia + DEB were more likely CSFaSynSAA+ (94% and 85%) vs RBD-Hyposmia (40%) and Hyposmia-DEB (55%). Among CSFaSynSAA+, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia + DEB had more mood, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms than Hyposmia-DEB. PPMI identified a large biologically-defined early neuronal synucleinopathy cohort and demonstrated biomarker and multi-domain clinical heterogeneity within CSFaSynSAA+ individuals prior to symptom onset.

papers.title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training.
papers.abstract: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.

papers.title: Non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and incident cardiovascular disease in obstructive sleep apnea: a prospective analysis of the Sleep Heart Health Study.
papers.abstract: Background Dyslipidemia is common in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and may contribute to its cardiovascular complications. The non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (NHHR) reflects the balance between atherogenic and anti-atherogenic cholesterol. However, its association with long-term cardiovascular risk in individuals with OSA remains unclear. We investigated the association between NHHR and incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) in adults with OSA. Methods This prospective analysis included 1,512 adults with OSA from the Sleep Heart Health Study. NHHR was analyzed continuously and by quartiles. Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine the association between NHHR and incident CVD, and restricted cubic splines were used to assess the dose-response relationship. Subgroup analyses were performed according to OSA severity and major metabolic characteristics. NHHR was also compared with the atherogenic index of plasma, lipid accumulation product, visceral adiposity index, and cardiometabolic index. Results During a median follow-up of 11.37 years, 344 participants developed incident CVD. After multivariable adjustment, each 1-standard deviation increase in NHHR was associated with a 26% higher risk of CVD (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.12-1.41; P < 0.001). Participants in the highest NHHR quartile had a 55% higher risk than those in the lowest quartile (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.12-2.13; P = 0.008). The association between NHHR and CVD was approximately linear (P overall = 0.001; P nonlinear = 0.445). The association was stronger in participants with severe OSA (HR per 1-SD 1.49, 95% CI 1.12-1.98), although the interaction across OSA severity was not significant. Stronger associations were also observed among participants with obesity and diabetes. Among the five lipid- and adiposity-related indices examined, NHHR showed the largest numerical improvement in model discrimination when added to conventional clinical factors. Conclusions Higher NHHR was associated with an increased long-term risk of incident CVD in adults with OSA. The association was more evident in participants with obesity or diabetes. As a simple index derived from routine lipid measurements, NHHR may provide additional information for cardiovascular risk assessment in OSA, particularly in individuals with accompanying metabolic abnormalities.

papers.title: Housing environmental enrichment influences mouse behavior and response to experimental metabolic disorders.
papers.abstract: Housing environmental is essential for animal welfare but may also influence the metabolic and behavioral outcomes of preclinical studies. This study investigates whether two commonly used enrichment materials, Nestlets and Sizzle, modify the effects of a high-fat diet (HFD) on metabolic and behavioral phenotypes in adult male C57BL/6 J mice. A total of 128 mice were fed either a normal diet (ND) or HFD for six months and housed in enriched cages containing either Nestlets (Nest) or Sizzle nesting material (n = 32 mice/condition). Metabolic parameters and behavioral performances were assessed at six months. Results show that HFD induced weight gain, hypercholesterolemia, fasting hyperglycemia, and impaired glucose tolerance under both enrichment conditions. However, Nest-enriched mice displayed lower cholesterol levels and differences in glycemic responses compared with Sizzle-enriched mice, suggesting that nesting material can modulate the severity of diet-induced metabolic alterations. Furthermore, environmental housing also affected behavior. Nest-enriched mice showed higher locomotor activity and reduced anxiety compared with Sizzle-enriched mice. Interestingly, HFD-induced impairment of visual recognition memory in the novel object recognition test was detected only in Nest-enriched mice. Overall, these findings demonstrate that different enrichment materials can substantially modify metabolic, emotional, motivational, and cognitive responses to HFD. These results highlight the need to carefully control and consistently maintain housing environmental conditions throughout long-term preclinical studies to improve reproducibility, interpretation of behavioral outcomes, and animal welfare.

papers.title: Reading the wrist as a mechanical observer of the collapsing pharynx: biomechanical inference of upper-airway soft tissue loading from wearable signals.
papers.abstract: The pharynx is a collapsible soft-tissue conduit whose patency is a mechanical equilibrium between intraluminal loading and tissue elastance, yet the transmural pressure that governs its collapse is accessible only through invasive laboratory manometry. Here, we reframe wearable sleep monitoring as inference over mechanically motivated surrogates of pharyngeal loading. From a Starling resistor and tube law description of pharyngeal collapse, we derive an explicit mapping from each wearable modality-photoplethysmography, electrocardiography, accelerometry, oximetry, and respiratory effort-to the mechanical term it is expected to reflect, casting the sensor array as a distributed set of mechanical observers of one collapse event. Three innovations follow: self-supervised pre-training restricted to mechanically admissible augmentations, retained only when a perturbed view remains a physically realizable airway state; a redundancy-aware fusion that combines correlated observers through a Sharpe-ratio-maximizing, closed-form weighting over their information covariance; and a proposed cumulative load index, formulated in the shape of a classical injury criterion, that summarizes a night of recording as an uncalibrated exposure to obstructive loading rather than an event count; the index is introduced as a hypothesis, not as a validated mechanical dose. Across two polysomnographic cohorts spanning ages 18-94, the framework surpasses 13 baselines in collapse detection and in three-way loading regime classification-sustained, absent, or delayed-onset loading-in both cohorts and retains its advantage when observers are lost, both under controlled channel dropout and under zero-shot transfer with only the two observers shared by the two corpora.

papers.title: Circadian clock components CCA1 and LHY shape heat responses across regulatory layers.
papers.abstract: High temperatures reprogram gene regulatory responses and are particularly deleterious for crop yield, especially when these events occur at night. This emphasizes that partitioning of heat responses is based on time of day. Coordination between time of day and environmental responses relies on the circadian clock. However, the precise regulatory mechanism of how the clock achieves this partitioning at different levels of gene regulation is poorly understood. Using circadian clock mutants with altered CCA1 and LHY expression, we generated a time-resolved transcriptome, proteome, and metabolome following a short-term heat stress in Arabidopsis. We identified regulatory connections specific to CCA1 and LHY, as well as those shared with other clock components linked to heat stress responses. Additionally, new connections between CCA1 and LHY and non-cycling genes highlight a broader role for the clock in regulating heat responsive gene expression. CCA1 and LHY regulated processes, such as sulfur assimilation and ROS scavenging, may contribute to time-of-day specific thermotolerance. Overall, heat responses were dampened in both the transcriptome and proteome in cca1lhy, suggesting both transcriptional and post-translational circadian-regulated processes are important for heat responses. Lastly, we identified differences in metabolic responses in cca1lhy and suggest a role for circadian regulation of starch degradation in thermotolerance. This study generates and utilizes data across levels of gene regulation to identify heat responses in the transcriptome and proteome regulated by CCA1 and LHY. These findings establish shared and distinct regulatory mechanisms of clock components in response to heat stress and provide new candidates for network integration and a foundation to engineer plants more tolerant to high temperatures depending on time of day.

papers.title: Psychosocial work conditions and the severity of insomnia symptoms and daytime sleepiness among nurses.
papers.abstract: Nurses are the largest occupational group in the healthcare system. Due to the nature of their work, they are particularly affected by consequences of changes occurring in the modern work environment. In this context, psychosocial working conditions are of particular importance, as they can either support employees' well-being and engagement or serve as a source of chronic stress. The aim of the study was to assess the associations between psychosocial working conditions and the severity of insomnia symptoms and daytime sleepiness among nurses, as well as to explore these associations across groups stratified by length of professional experience. The study included 366 male and female nurses from all over Poland. A diagnostic survey method was employed, utilizing the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) and the Psychosocial Working Conditions Questionnaire as well as a proprietary questionnaire that covered socio-demographic and work-related data. Statistical analysis was performed using non-parametric tests. The results of the study indicate that higher job demands were significantly associated with higher education (rho = 0.138; p = 0.008), more years of practice in the profession (rho = 0.153; p = 0.003), more years of practice at the current workplace (rho = 0.113; p = 0.030), a higher number of working hours per week (rho = 0.238; p < 0.001), a higher number of additional jobs (rho = 0.175; p = 0.001), and more frequent overtime work (rho = 0.135; p = 0.010). At the same time, higher job demands were associated with fewer patients per nurse during a shift. Among nurses with less than 5 years of professional experience, high job demands and well-being were significantly associated with the severity of sleep disturbances. Greater job control was associated with lower insomnia severity, whereas higher job demands were associated with greater severity of both insomnia and daytime sleepiness. Exploratory analyses conducted separately across professional experience groups revealed different patterns of correlations between dimensions of psychosocial working conditions and the severity of insomnia and daytime sleepiness. These analyses did not include a formal comparison of the strength of associations between the groups. Higher levels of well-being, greater job control, and higher levels of social support were associated with less severe sleep problems in some analyses. Higher job demands were associated with more severe insomnia symptoms in some analyses and with a greater working-time burden, including longer working hours and more frequent overtime. Given the cross-sectional design and exploratory analyses, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

papers.title: Meditation-induced coherence and perennial aging.
papers.abstract: This article investigates the effects of meditation on human physiological processes using a non-Markovian quantum-like approach compatible with self-organization and the breakdown of ergodicity of ordinary statistical physics. According to the theory of self-organization, these processes are nonergodic and exhibit finite survival. Their scaling behavior is characterized by the parameter δ , ranging from a minimal value of δ = 0 to a maximal value of δ = 1 . The condition of maximal cognition, δ = 1 , represents an idealized limit, as suggested by the relation μ R = 2 - δ , corresponding to unbounded survival ( μ R = 1 ) . Meditation appears to reduce the scaling exponent δ during the meditative state while promoting neural coherence, a property that, in the case of Naam Jap meditation, is attributed entirely to crucial events. During Naam Jap meditation, the decrease in δ is observed in both brain and heart dynamics and is accompanied by enhanced brain-heart complexity synchronization. Following this meditation-induced coherent state, δ increases above its pre-meditation value, with group-level statistical analysis supporting this increase in both electroencephalogram (EEG) and electrocardiogram (ECG) dynamics, suggesting a post-meditation enhancement of physiological complexity. These results further suggest that the scaling exponent δ depends on an inverse power-law index μ , following δ = μ - 1 for μ < 2 and δ = 1 / ( μ - 1 ) for μ > 2 , with δ = 0.5 for μ > 3 . We focus on the μ < 2 regime, a condition of perennial ergodicity breaking that is of fundamental importance for understanding the interaction between different physiological processes. For an illustrative subject, different analytical approaches yield μ ≃ 1.83 , supporting the robustness of the scaling behavior and its characterization by μ < 2 . Maximal survival corresponds to the limiting condition μ = 2 , while environmental noise prevents the unbounded survival of self-organized processes; for μ ≃ 1.83 , we obtain μ R ≃ 1.17 . These results are expected to offer a new perspective on the open field of cognition.

papers.title: Associations of night-shift sleep and recovery experiences with occupational fatigue among emergency nurses: a multicenter cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Emergency nurses experience substantial occupational demands, including night work and irregular schedules, which may disrupt sleep and recovery. Occupational fatigue is multidimensional, encompassing chronic fatigue, acute fatigue, and intershift recovery. However, the roles of post-night-shift sleep characteristics and recovery experiences in different fatigue dimensions remain unclear. This study investigated their associations with occupational fatigue among emergency nurses. A multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted among emergency nurses from several hospitals in Taizhou, Zhejiang Province, China, in late July 2026. Participants completed a self-administered electronic questionnaire assessing demographic and occupational characteristics, night-shift sleep characteristics, recovery experiences, occupational fatigue, and work-family conflict. Recovery experience was measured using the Recovery Experience Questionnaire (REQ), and occupational fatigue was assessed using the Occupational Fatigue Exhaustion/Recovery Scale (OFER-15). Multivariable linear regression models were constructed for chronic fatigue, acute fatigue, and intershift recovery, with adjustment for demographic, occupational, and work-family conflict covariates. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess robustness. The study included 216 emergency nurses. Higher REQ overall mean scores were associated with lower chronic fatigue (B = -0.523, 95% CI -0.857 to -0.189), lower acute fatigue (B = -0.703, 95% CI -0.961 to -0.444), and better intershift recovery (B = 0.582, 95% CI 0.327 to 0.836). Compared with sleep-onset latency <15 min, latencies of 31-60 min and >60 min were associated with poorer intershift recovery. Fragmented sleep showed a positive but not statistically significant association with acute fatigue in the primary analysis (B = 0.365, 95% CI -0.022 to 0.751, P = 0.064). Neither average monthly night shifts nor shift-system categories were significantly associated with the three outcomes. Higher recovery experience scores were associated with lower fatigue and better intershift recovery among emergency nurses. Sleep-onset latencies of 31-60 min and >60 min were associated with poorer intershift recovery compared with <15 min. No statistically significant associations with monthly night-shift frequency or shift-system categories were detected in the primary models. Future longitudinal studies incorporating objective sleep and circadian measures are warranted.

papers.title: Label-Free Lymphocyte Subtype and State Classification by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy.
papers.abstract: Accurate immune cell subtype and functional state profiling are essential for studying immune regulation, disease progression, and therapeutic response. Established single-cell analysis techniques rely heavily on either endpoint, destructive measurements or complex labeling that can potentially affect cell functions. Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy offers quantitative, label-free imaging of cells and tissues by providing contrast based on subcellular concentrations of intrinsic biomolecules at high spatial and temporal resolution. Here, we demonstrate that Vision Transformer based hyperspectral SRS imaging classification can accurately and non-destructively classify various lymphocyte phenotypes, including lymphocyte lineage (T and B cells), T cell subset and differentiation state (CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, effector, memory, and naïve for both), and functional states (naïve T, activated T, exhausted T) using fluorescent markers for training. By leveraging attention-based spatial-spectral feature learning, the approach captures biomolecular patterns associated with immune-cell identity and state while preserving cells for downstream or longitudinal analysis. This provides a potential platform for label-free immune profiling, live-cell analysis, and longitudinal studies of immune cell type and state transitions.

papers.title: Participant Motivation and Experience in a Prospective Study of 24-Hour Movement During Pregnancy.
papers.abstract: Background Understanding participant perspectives about participation in research on health behaviors during pregnancy is important for optimizing recruitment, engagement, and retention. Although prior research has examined the feasibility of studying health behaviors during pregnancy using wearable devices and self-report measures, less is known about participant motivations and experiences with study procedures. We examined participant-reported motivations and feedback from a longitudinal study assessing physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep during pregnancy using wearable devices, sleep diaries, and self-report measures. Methods Participants with pre-pregnancy overweight or obesity enrolled in the 24MOVE prospective cohort study completed assessments at three timepoints during pregnancy. After completing all study activities, participants were invited to complete a feedback survey assessing motivations for participation and experiences with recruitment and informed consent materials, study procedures, wearable device use, and data collection activities. Open-ended responses were reviewed by three co-authors to identify recurring themes in participant motivations and feedback. Quantitative responses were summarized using frequencies and percentages. Results Among 305 participants enrolled in the study, 180 (59%) completed the feedback survey. Three primary themes emerged from open-ended responses: altruistic motivations, including contributing to research and improving outcomes for pregnant individuals; incentive-driven motivations, including financial compensation; and personal motivations, including interest in tracking health, physical activity, and sleep during pregnancy. Most participants reported that recruitment and informed consent materials prepared them for participation (94.4%) and that instructions for wearing the device were easy to understand and follow (98.9%). Previous-night sleep questions were generally perceived as easy to respond to (95.0%), whereas device comfort received more mixed feedback, particularly during nighttime wear. Participants identified diet and activity recall surveys as the most burdensome study activities and suggested app-based or real-time data collection, shorter surveys, and improvements in device comfort. Conclusions Participants were motivated by a combination of altruistic, personal, and financial factors. Although study procedures were generally well received, device comfort and survey burden were important areas for improvement. Incorporating participant-informed strategies, including more comfortable wearable devices and streamlined, technology-enabled data collection methods, may improve participant experience and support recruitment, engagement, and retention in pregnancy research.

papers.title: Compensatory drive and sleep-related phantom limb pain: the moderating role of autonomic reserve.
papers.abstract: Phantom limb pain (PLP) is highly prevalent, yet the link between poor sleep and PLP remains poorly understood. Because regulatory systems depend on available physiologic reserves, we tested if autonomic capacity moderates the sleep-pain relationship in 121 amputee adults. Sleep was assessed with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; PLP, residual limb pain (RLP), and phantom limb sensation (PLS) on 0-10 scales. Heart rate variability was summarized as autonomic reserve (log-transformed SDNN, RMSSD, total and high-frequency power) and autonomic drive (normalized low-frequency power). Poorer sleep was associated with greater PLP and RLP, but not PLS. No single HRV index moderated these associations, but the sleep × reserve × drive interaction did for PLP (b = - 0.51, p = 0.026). Poor sleep predicted pain most strongly under high drive with reduced reserve. PLP vulnerability reflects autonomic capacity relative to demand, instead of any single HRV marker alone.

papers.title: Distinct neurophysiological signatures of guided visual search in schizophrenia and autism: Evidence from fixation-related potentials, alpha modulation, and functional MRI.
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are associated with convergent differences in social perception relative to non-autistic, non-schizophrenia controls (NC), but divergent patterns of alterations in early visual activity. Here, we used multimodal imaging during the Guided Visual Search task to investigate the differential patterns of early visual alteration across SZ and ASD including superior colliculus (SC) and pulvinar nucleus. In Experiment 1, simultaneous eye tracking and EEG were obtained from 91 individuals (35 NC, 20 ASD, 36 SZ). Fixation-related potential (FRP) was time-locked to fixation onset. In Experiment 2, fMRI during Guided Search was obtained from a partly overlapping sample of 71 individuals (27 NC, 25 ASD, 19 SZ). In behavioral analyses, SZ was associated with significantly prolonged search time (d=.74, p=.003), which was attributable primarily to reduced mean saccade amplitude, whereas ASD was associated with a small advantage (d=.35), which was not statistically significant. In EEG analyses, SZ was associated with reduced amplitude of the FRP P1 (lambda) response (d=1.15, p<.0001) relative to NC that remained significant following control for saccade size (p<.0001), but with normal task-related modulation of background alpha activity. In contrast, ASD was associated with normal FRP amplitude and larger alpha suppression (d=.83, p=.007) that was attributable to increased alpha levels during pre-task fixation (at matched pre-onset alpha levels, d=.14, p=.66). Within SZ, P1 correlated with the MCCB composite (r=.56, p=.001). Within ASD, ADOS-2 Communication correlated with P1 (r=.51, p=.024) and with the broadband change from pre-onset to search (r=-.51, p=.030). In fMRI, SZ was associated with correlated activation reductions in the Visual1 (Sidak p<.001) and Visual2 (Sidak p=.022) networks and SC (Sidak p=.019), whereas activation was unaffected in the Dorsal Attention and Frontoparietal networks, Frontal Eye Fields and pulvinar. In ASD, activation was increased in pulvinar (Sidak p≤.038), but unaffected elsewhere. Cortical activation patterns associated with SC activation resembled those associated with P1 generation across groups. Overall, the findings support bottom-up disturbances of visual processing in schizophrenia. In autism, pre-onset alpha was higher and task-related suppression was larger.

papers.title: Expanded representation and function of PDF neurons in the mosquito circadian network.
papers.abstract: Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can transmit pathogens when they bite humans, their preferred hosts, and this host-seeking drive is tightly gated by time of day. Daily rhythms depend on the molecular clock and communication among clock neurons, yet mosquito circadian network organization remains poorly understood. Using a mosquito-specific PERIOD antibody, we mapped the putative clock network of Aedes aegypti and found that neurons expressing the neuropeptide Pigment-Dispersing Factor (PDF) make up a much larger proportion of clock neurons compared to other insects, indicating a divergent network organization. PDF neurons are required for normal rhythms across insects, but whether their importance scales with their abundance in the network is unknown. We therefore tested the functional role of this expanded PDF neuron population in mosquitoes: we show that electrically silencing Aedes aegypti PDF neurons abolished the separation of daily activity into morning and evening peaks and led to misaligned clock protein rhythms across circadian neurons, even under entraining light-dark cycles. Thus, in a network built around an unusually large PDF population, PDF neuron activity plays an outsized role in behavioral timing and network synchrony.

papers.title: Prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling promotes maladaptive plasticity of direct pathway striatal projection neurons.
papers.abstract: As Parkinson's disease (PD) progresses and nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neuron degeneration worsens, DA replacement therapies shift from restoring motor function to evoking dyskinesia. How disease progression mediates this transition remains poorly understood. Here, we optimized a 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) model that reliably generates multiple severities of DA axon denervation within the striatum of individual mice. We identify a critical denervation threshold at which direct-pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), which are key drivers of dyskinesia become pathologically hyperresponsive to DA. Using slice electrophysiology, we establish that denervation-induced increase in intrinsic excitability is insufficient to explain the aberrant response of dSPNs to DA. We further demonstrate using genetic and chemogenetic manipulations that prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling drives the pathological transformation of dSPNs cell-autonomously, and that sustained G s -coupled metabotropic receptor signaling in dSPNs is sufficient to both prevent and reverse it. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how PD progression renders striatal circuits vulnerable to DA-evoked motor complications and identify sustained signaling by G s -coupled receptors as a potential avenue for preventing or reversing denervation-induced maladaptive striatal plasticity. dSPN hyperactivation in response to DA treatments emerges only when local DA axons are completely lostIncreased dSPN intrinsic excitability emerges at intermediate denervation and, as such, cannot explain the shift in DA responsiveness when denervation is complete Cell-autonomous deletion of D1 receptors reproduces the pathological shift in dSPN responsiveness to G s -coupled metabotropic signaling Sustained G s -coupled metabotropic signaling prevents and reverses denervation-induced maladaptive plasticity in dSPNs.

papers.title: Chronic evoked seizures differentially worsen cognitive function and long-term neuropsychiatric comorbidities in Alzheimer's disease-related genotypes.
papers.abstract: Variants in one of three deterministic risk genes - amyloid precursor protein (APP), presenilin 1 (PSEN1), or presenilin 2 (PSEN2) - lead to early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD), which also carries a high risk of spontaneous seizures. Seizures may worsen AD-related behavioral comorbidities, including depression, anxiety, and cognitive impairment. Using the corneal kindling model of secondarily generalized focal seizures in two distinct aged male and female EOAD-associated mouse models, we assessed the interaction between investigator-initiated chronic seizures and EOAD genotype on AD-related behavioral comorbidities. Genotypes were selected to model amyloid-β independent and dependent AD risk factors and included: PSEN2-N141I (amyloid-β independent model) versus wild-type (PSEN2 control) mice, and APP/PS1 (amyloid-β dependent model) versus wild-type littermates (Tg-). Sham and fully kindled mice then underwent behavioral assessment in the saccharin preference test of anhedonia-like behavior, the Barnes maze test of spatial learning and memory, and a 67-hour home cage monitoring of circadian activity. EOAD genotype only significantly affected kindling acquisition of aged APP/PS1 females. However, there was no significant genotype or kindling effect on saccharin preference, suggesting no adverse impact on anhedonia-like behavior. Cognitive performance in the Barnes maze was significantly worsened by seizures exclusively in APP/PS1 female mice. However, seizures generally worsened Barnes maze performance of male PSEN2-N141I and PSEN2 control mice. Finally, chronic seizures consistently worsened exploratory behavior patterns during home cage circadian activity monitoring exclusively in APP/PS1 male and female mice. This study reveals the AD-related heterogeneity of seizure-evoked behavioral consequences on spatial working memory and circadian behaviors.

papers.title: Multisensory brain processing is associated with depressive symptoms in youth with chronic pain.
papers.abstract: Juvenile fibromyalgia (JFM) is a chronic pain condition marked by widespread musculoskeletal pain and often accompanied by physical fatigue, nonrestorative sleep, headaches, anxiety, and depression. Previous studies have found that adolescents with fibromyalgia report augmented unpleasantness and altered brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimuli. Likewise, research in major depression has shown altered neural processing of sensory stimulation. We examined whether augmented brain responses to non-painful multisensory stimulation is associated with depressive symptoms in adolescent girls with JFM. Forty-six female adolescents with JFM (mean ± SD, 16.43 ± 1.10 years [range 13-18 years]) and 44 healthy participants (mean ± SD, 16.09 ± 1.06 years [range 13-18 years]) completed validated questionnaires assessing daily-life sensory hypersensitivity and depressive symptoms, alongside undergoing a functional MRI multisensory task. JFM patients reported significantly higher sensory unpleasantness than healthy participants, and this hypersensitivity was positively associated with depressive symptoms. Neuroimaging results in chronic pain patients revealed that greater depressive symptomatology was associated with increased activation in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) (p FWE <0.05), a region implicated in self-referential processing and specifically rumination in adults with chronic pain. JFM patients showed increased PCC-left middle temporal gyrus task-dependent connectivity using psychophysiological interactions analysis (PPI). Furthermore, hyperconnectivity between the PCC and brain areas involved in cognitive-affective regulation, sensory integration, and memory processing was strongly correlated with depressive symptoms in JFM patients. These findings underscore the role of depressive symptoms in sensory processing and integration in JFM patients and highlight the complex interplay between sensory processing and emotional/self-referential brain function in patients.

papers.title: Timing the Target: Exploring the Circadian Transcriptome of Biologic Therapies in Asthma.
papers.abstract: Many of the immune pathways involved in asthma or in asthma treatment show circadian or diurnal variation. Understanding this variation can aid in biomarker discovery and/or therapy optimization. To evaluate if receptors, cytokines, and their pathways (n=46) targeted by currently approved biologics show significant diurnal rhythmicity and to identify their peak expression time. We used longitudinal bulk RNA sequencing datasets (discovery/replication cohorts: GSE113883 and GSE223613) and one microarray file (GSE39445) for cross-platform replication/validation. First, we used 16 canonical clock genes (including CLOCK , BMAL1 , REV-ERBß ) as positive controls to explore rhythmicity in each cohort. Thereafter, we evaluated if any targets of currently approved biologics or their corresponding receptors showed significant diurnal variation. For significant genes (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR<0.05), we estimated the baseline average, phase, peak-time of expression across the 24-hour day using clock time and quantified the cross-cohort consistency in the peak time of expression across the cohorts. These cohorts included 453 longitudinal samples collected every two to four hours over a 24-28h cycle. Twelve (75%) of 16 evaluable clock genes showed significant rhythmicity. Only 34 of 46 (74%) asthma-related genes were evaluable across two or more cohorts. Of these 34 genes, 23 (68%) showed significant variation. Across all cohorts, the most preserved rhythmically expressed targets included many pathways or targets of monoclonal antibodies that are currently approved or in development: GATA3 and STAT6 , master regulators of type 2 inflammation and IL4/IL13 signaling; chemokines, including the neutrophil chemoattractant, CXCL8 ; IL-5RA , benralizumab's target; FcRE1 , suppressed by omalizumab; and IL1RL1 ( ST2 ) in clinical trials. Many therapeutic targets in asthma show significant diurnal rhythmicity. Future studies on how dosing time affects their therapeutic effectiveness while minimizing side effects are needed. Many targets of biologics and their pathways are significantly rhythmic in expression across the day. This includes IL5RA , transcription factors, like STAT6 and GATA3 , and the high-affinity IgE receptor. Asthma may be a prime area for chronotherapy. Longitudinal transcriptomics data show that many targets of currently available biologics and their pathways are significantly rhythmic in expression across the day. The circadian transcriptome includes surface receptors like IL5RA , targeted by benralizumab, and transcription factors, like STAT6 and GATA3 , master regulators of Th2 differentiation involved in the IL-4/-13 pathway targeted by dupilumab, and the high affinity IgE receptor suppressed by omalizumab. Monoclonal antibody therapy in asthma may be a prime area for investigating chronotherapy in asthma.

papers.title: State-dependent gating of sensory and cortical inputs by median raphe neurons.
papers.abstract: The mesopontine median raphe (MnR) plays an important role in regulating brain states, hippocampal network activity, and memory processes. Recent studies have revealed that the MnR comprises three major neuronal populations: serotonergic (5-HT), glutamatergic (Vglut3-expressing), and GABAergic neurons. How these distinct neuronal populations may gate sensory and cortical inputs across different brain states remains largely unknown. Here, we combined in vivo electrophysiological recording, sensory or optogenetic stimulation, and transgenic approaches to characterize the response properties of 5-HT, Vglut3, and GABAergic MnR neurons during wakefulness and sleep. We found that MnR neurons exhibited pronounced state-dependent responses to both sensory and cortical stimulation, with response amplitudes significantly greater during slow-wave sleep than during wakefulness. Auditory and somatosensory stimuli elicited fast responses in the MnR: 5-HT neurons were primarily suppressed, whereas Vglut3 and GABAergic neurons were primarily activated, suggesting the presence of direct inputs from sensory thalamic or brainstem structures. Retrograde tracing identified several brainstem structures and, notably, the medial prefrontal cortex as sources of direct projections to the MnR. Optogenetic stimulation of prefrontal inputs to the MnR evoked inhibition of 5-HT neurons but robust excitation of Vglut3 neurons during slow-wave sleep, suggesting top-down control of MnR activity by the prefrontal cortex. Together, these findings reveal that the MnR exhibits enhanced sensitivity to both ascending sensory and descending cortical inputs during sleep, suggesting that it may integrate environmental and cortical signals to regulate hippocampal network activity and gate sleep-dependent memory processing.

papers.title: The Effects of Hand Massage on Agitated Behaviors in Older Adults with Dementia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: This study investigated the effects of hand massage on agitated behaviors in older adults with dementia. This randomized controlled trial included 66 residents (intervention: n = 32; control: n = 34) in dementia group homes and long-term care welfare facilities. The intervention group received six 10-min bedtime hand massage sessions over 2 weeks, whereas the control group received standard care. Agitated behaviors were assessed using the Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory (CMAI), and sleep patterns were monitored via non-contact sheet-type sensors. The between-group difference in total CMAI scores (primary outcome) was not statistically significant. However, the intervention group showed a significant reduction in the "non-aggressive behaviors" subcategory compared with the control group (p < .05). No significant group × time interactions were observed for objective sleep parameters. No intervention-related adverse events were observed. Although total CMAI scores (the primary outcome) showed no significant difference, hand massage significantly reduced non-aggressive behaviors (a secondary outcome). These findings suggest that bedtime hand massage may be a feasible non-pharmacological option for addressing non-aggressive behaviors. Bedtime hand massage may be a feasible non-pharmacological option for addressing non-aggressive behaviors in dementia care settings.

papers.title: Beyond attention tasks: Adolescent sleep debt, social jetlag, and the urgent case for school start time reform.
Integrating diagnosis, classification, and multimodal management in epilepsy care.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder marked by a predisposition to unprovoked seizures, often described as sudden "electrical storms" in the brain. The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) defines it as a disorder encompassing not only seizures but also their neurobiological, cognitive, psychological, and social impacts. Affecting about 50 million people worldwide, epilepsy presents a public health challenge in low- and middle-income countries, with treatment gaps exceeding 75%. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, witness accounts, and diagnostic tools such as electroencephalograms (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to differentiate between focal and generalized seizures. This review aims to highlight first-line management options, including anti-seizure medications (ASMs), surgical interventions for drug-resistant cases, dietary therapies such as the ketogenic diet, and device-based neuromodulation, such as vagus nerve stimulation (VNS). We synthesize evidence on epilepsy epidemiology, seizure classification, clinical manifestations, diagnostic pathways, and treatment modalities, while addressing the psychosocial burden and quality-of-life implications associated with the disorder. Integrated diagnostic approaches combining clinical history, seizure semiology, EEG, and MRI can improve epilepsy classification and etiological identification. ASMs achieve effective seizure control in approximately 60-70% of diagnosed patients, while a substantial subset develops drug-resistant epilepsy. Surgical intervention can provide greater long-term seizure freedom compared with continued pharmacotherapy. Dietary therapies and neuromodulation techniques, including VNS and deep brain stimulation, can reduce seizure frequency and severity. Genetic testing, AI-assisted EEG analysis, and digital monitoring may enhance diagnostic precision, treatment stratification, and quality of life through personalized, multidisciplinary care models. Epilepsy management is evolving toward a personalized, precision-medicine framework driven by advances in genetics, biomarkers, AI-assisted diagnostics, and digital health technologies for continuous monitoring. A holistic, multidisciplinary care model should integrate optimized seizure control with cognitive, psychological, and social support.
